claim: Neurons in sensory systems reduce responses to sustained stimuli.
source: Neural circuits in sensory systems have been shown to reduce responses to sustained stimuli (Adrian and Zotterman, 1926; Albrecht et al., 1984; Maffei et al., 1973)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Neural responses to sustained stimuli adapt over the course of a few seconds in visual cortex.
source: In visual cortex, neural responses to a sustained stimulus adapt over the course of a few seconds.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific understanding

claim: Most experiments on adaptation were carried out in anesthetized animals.
source: Most experiments on adaptation, however, were carried out in anesthetized animals.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field

claim: Responses of neurons in anaesthetized mouse primary visual cortex adapt to sustained high-contrast grating stimuli.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Ahmed et al., 1997; Carandini and Ferster, 1997; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2000; Vidyasagar, 1990; Keller and Martin, 2015), we found that the responses of neurons in anaesthetized mouse primary visual cortex (V1) adapt to sustained high-contrast grating stimuli (Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1 showing experimental data

claim: Contrast adaptation in anesthetized mouse V1 depends on local cortical activity.
source: this adaptation depends on local cortical activity (King et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: Tonic feedforward inhibition mediated by parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneurons is a proposed mechanism underlying contrast adaptation.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed to underlie such contrast adaptation (Ahmed et al., 1997; Carandini and Ferster, 1997; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2000; Vidyasagar, 1990; Keller and Martin, 2015), including tonic feedforward inhibition mediated by parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneurons (Ahmed et al., 1997; Keller and Martin, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: PV+ neurons adapt less than putative excitatory neurons under anesthesia.
source: Accordingly, we found that PV+ neurons adapt less than putative excitatory neurons and that adaptation is only weakly orientation-specific for both neuron types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: Adaptation is only weakly orientation-specific for both PV+ and putative excitatory neuron types under anesthesia.
source: Accordingly, we found that PV+ neurons adapt less than putative excitatory neurons and that adaptation is only weakly orientation-specific for both neuron types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: Adaptation was absent in awake mice during sustained grating presentations.
source: As opposed to data obtained under anesthesia, we found that adaptation was absent and neural activity even increased during sustained grating presentations in awake recordings (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2i–l, 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by reference to multiple figures showing experimental data

claim: Neural activity increased during sustained grating presentations in awake mice.
source: As opposed to data obtained under anesthesia, we found that adaptation was absent and neural activity even increased during sustained grating presentations in awake recordings (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2i–l, 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by reference to multiple figures showing experimental data

claim: Adaptation was stronger for almost all cells in anesthetized compared to awake mice.
source: Adaptation was stronger (i.e. slope of adaptation more negative) for almost all cells in anesthetized compared to awake mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: The reversal of adaptation in awake mice could not be explained by response saturation.
source: This reversal of adaptation in awake mice could be explained neither by response saturation, nor locomotion, nor eye movements (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplements 2i,k and 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: The reversal of adaptation in awake mice could not be explained by locomotion.
source: This reversal of adaptation in awake mice could be explained neither by response saturation, nor locomotion, nor eye movements (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplements 2i,k and 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: The reversal of adaptation in awake mice could not be explained by eye movements.
source: This reversal of adaptation in awake mice could be explained neither by response saturation, nor locomotion, nor eye movements (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplements 2i,k and 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to figures showing experimental data

claim: An attentional mechanism could prevent adaptation when a stimulus is of unknown relevance to the animal.
source: We hypothesize that an attentional mechanism could prevent adaptation when a stimulus is of unknown relevance to the animal.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis

claim: Adaptation should reappear if mice divert attention away from the stimulus and learn that the stimulus is behaviorally irrelevant.
source: If so, adaptation should reappear if mice divert attention away from the stimulus and learn that the stimulus is behaviorally irrelevant.
evidence: Stated as a prediction based on the hypothesis

claim: Adaptation to the grating stimulus was absent initially when mice were learning the navigation task.
source: Consistent with the lack of adaptation in the passively observing awake mouse (Figure 1), we found that adaptation to the grating stimulus was absent initially.
evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1

claim: Adaptation of neural responses to the grating stimulus reappeared as mice learned to perform the navigation task in the grating-irrelevant condition.
source: As mice learned to perform the navigation task, however, adaptation of neural responses to the grating stimulus reappeared ('grating-irrelevant' condition, Figure 2e,g,h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to figures and video showing experimental data

claim: The reappearance of adaptation suggests that mice diverted attention away from the grating stimulus as they learned to interact with the task-relevant part of the visual field.
source: This reappearance of adaptation suggests that mice, as they learned to interact with the task-relevant part of the visual field, diverted attention away from the grating stimulus that contained no task-relevant information.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: Adaptation remained absent over training sessions in the grating-relevant group.
source: We found that adaptation remained absent over training sessions in the grating-relevant group, despite visual experience being identical to the grating-irrelevant group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing two groups

claim: When mice exhibited anticipatory licking to the reward, neural responses showed an effect opposite to adaptation and activity increased over the course of the stimulus presentation.
source: Moreover, when mice exhibited anticipatory licking to the reward, neural responses showed an effect opposite to adaptation and activity increased over the course of the stimulus presentation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–i).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: The differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in mean running speed.
source: We verified that the differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in mean running speed, time spent running or number of saccades (Figure 2—figure supplement 2j–l).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: The differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in time spent running.
source: We verified that the differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in mean running speed, time spent running or number of saccades (Figure 2—figure supplement 2j–l).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: The differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in number of saccades.
source: We verified that the differences in adaptation between the grating-relevant group and the grating-irrelevant group cannot be explained by learning-related changes in mean running speed, time spent running or number of saccades (Figure 2—figure supplement 2j–l).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary figure showing experimental data

claim: In behaving animals, contrast adaptation is modulated bidirectionally by stimulus relevance.
source: These results suggest, therefore, that in behaving animals contrast adaptation is modulated bidirectionally by stimulus relevance (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,i).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results with reference to supplementary figure

claim: The responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1 do not adapt to sustained stimuli that are behaviorally relevant.
source: Thus, the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1 do not adapt to sustained stimuli that are behaviorally relevant, but they do adapt if the stimulus within their receptive field is irrelevant and animals learn to direct attention away from it to other parts of the visual field.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1 adapt if the stimulus within their receptive field is irrelevant and animals learn to direct attention away from it to other parts of the visual field.
source: Thus, the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1 do not adapt to sustained stimuli that are behaviorally relevant, but they do adapt if the stimulus within their receptive field is irrelevant and animals learn to direct attention away from it to other parts of the visual field.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The attentional modulation of adaptation effects are likely mediated by attentional mechanisms.
source: These effects are likely mediated by attentional mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016) that could directly enhance the responses to relevant stimuli to prevent adaptation.
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to prior research

claim: Attentional mechanisms could directly enhance the responses to relevant stimuli to prevent adaptation.
source: These effects are likely mediated by attentional mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016) that could directly enhance the responses to relevant stimuli to prevent adaptation.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on interpretation of results

claim: The attentional modulation of adaptation was not simply explained by changes in the adaptation of inhibitory neurons.
source: The attentional modulation of adaptation was also not simply explained by changes in the adaptation of inhibitory neurons (data not shown) and is unlikely to be generated only locally.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown)

claim: The attentional modulation of adaptation is unlikely to be generated only locally.
source: The attentional modulation of adaptation was also not simply explained by changes in the adaptation of inhibitory neurons (data not shown) and is unlikely to be generated only locally.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: fMRI studies on awake humans have found response adaptation in V1 upon the presentation of visual patterns.
source: In contrast to our findings in mouse V1, fMRI studies on awake humans have found response adaptation in V1 upon the presentation of visual patterns (Gardner et al., 2005; Fang et al., 2005; Huk and Heeger, 2001, but see Kastner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The disparity between mouse V1 findings and human fMRI studies is likely the result of small but relevant differences in study design.
source: This disparity is likely the result of small but relevant differences in study design.
evidence: Interpretation of differences between studies

claim: Huk and Heeger (2001) found weak adaptation in V1 when participants were attending to two separate moving plaid stimuli.
source: For example, Huk and Heeger (2001) find a weak adaptation in V1 when participants were attending to two separate moving plaid stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Distributing attention decreases attentional effects.
source: This could be explained by the fact that distributing attention decreases attentional effects (Ito and Gilbert, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Some fMRI studies used stimuli that are known to cause adaptation in thalamus and even the retina.
source: Other studies (Gardner et al., 2005; Fang et al., 2005) used stimuli that are known to cause adaptation in thalamus and even the retina (Smirnakis et al., 1997; Chander and Chichilnisky, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Some fMRI studies cannot distinguish the effects of cortical adaptation from those of subcortical adaptation.
source: Other studies (Gardner et al., 2005; Fang et al., 2005) used stimuli that are known to cause adaptation in thalamus and even the retina (Smirnakis et al., 1997; Chander and Chichilnisky, 2001) and cannot distinguish the effects of cortical adaptation from those of subcortical adaptation.
evidence: Interpretation of limitations of prior studies

claim: Adaptation is dynamically regulated by task demand during learning.
source: In summary, we have shown that adaptation is dynamically regulated by task demand during learning.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Cortex dynamically regulates the flow of sensory information by suppressing responses to non-relevant stimuli through mechanisms of adaptation.
source: Our data are consistent with the idea that cortex dynamically regulates the flow of sensory information by suppressing responses to non-relevant stimuli through mechanisms of adaptation, while boosting sensory responses that are behaviorally important.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Cortex boosts sensory responses that are behaviorally important.
source: Our data are consistent with the idea that cortex dynamically regulates the flow of sensory information by suppressing responses to non-relevant stimuli through mechanisms of adaptation, while boosting sensory responses that are behaviorally important.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Anesthetized mice show a significantly more negative slope of adaptation compared to awake mice.
source: Anesthetized mice show a significantly more negative slope compared to all other states [anest. (169 cells) – awake (169 cells): p<10−10; Wilcoxon signed-rank; running (51 cells): p<10−4; resting (169 cells): p<10−10; eye movements (168 cells): p<10−10; eye movement-free (165 cells): p<10−10; Wilcoxon rank-sum].
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was no significant difference in adaptation slope between running and resting mice.
source: There was no significant difference between running and resting mice, as opposed to the significant but small difference in eye movement and eye movement-free trials (p=0.49 and p=0.0047, respectively; Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was a significant but small difference in adaptation slope between eye movement and eye movement-free trials.
source: There was no significant difference between running and resting mice, as opposed to the significant but small difference in eye movement and eye movement-free trials (p=0.49 and p=0.0047, respectively; Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The LED+adapted condition evokes similar spike rates compared to the control condition in putative excitatory cells.
source: The LED+adapted condition evokes similar spike rates compared to the control and significantly more than the adapted condition (tuned putative excitatory: 109 cells; LED+adapted/adapted: p<10−10; LED+adapted/control: p=0.13; adapted/control: p<10−10; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The LED+adapted condition evokes significantly more spike activity than the adapted condition in putative excitatory cells.
source: The LED+adapted condition evokes similar spike rates compared to the control and significantly more than the adapted condition (tuned putative excitatory: 109 cells; LED+adapted/adapted: p<10−10; LED+adapted/control: p=0.13; adapted/control: p<10−10; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: All stimulus conditions evoke similar spike rates in PV+ neurons.
source: All conditions evoke similar spike rates (tuned PV+: 27 cells; LED+adapted/adapted: p=0.73; LED+adapted/control: p=0.067; adapted/control: p=0.17; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: PV+ neurons adapt significantly less than putative excitatory cells under anesthesia as measured by electrophysiology.
source: Adaptation is quantified as the mean decrease in the normalized spike rate per second during the stimulus presentation (tuned putative excitatory: 109 cells; PV+: 27 cells; p=0.010; Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: PV+ neurons adapt significantly less than putative excitatory cells under anesthesia as measured by two-photon calcium imaging.
source: Adaptation is quantified as the mean decrease in normalized ∆F/F per second during the stimulus presentation (tuned putative excitatory: 545 cells; PV+: 78 cells; p=3.7×10−4; Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Iso-orientation adaptation differs significantly from cross-orientation adaptation at 25% contrast in putative excitatory cells under anesthesia.
source: Iso-orientation compared to cross-orientation adaptation (50% contrast) of tuned putative excitatory cells measured at 25% or 100% contrast. This is quantified as average ∆F/F after adaptation (seconds 11–12; indicated by the vertical dotted lines in e; 299 cells; 25%: p<10−10; 100%: p<10−4; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Iso-orientation adaptation differs significantly from cross-orientation adaptation at 100% contrast in putative excitatory cells under anesthesia.
source: Iso-orientation compared to cross-orientation adaptation (50% contrast) of tuned putative excitatory cells measured at 25% or 100% contrast. This is quantified as average ∆F/F after adaptation (seconds 11–12; indicated by the vertical dotted lines in e; 299 cells; 25%: p<10−10; 100%: p<10−4; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There is no significant difference between iso- and cross-orientation adaptation in PV+ cells under anesthesia at 25% or 100% contrast.
source: Same as f but for PV+ cells (40 cells; 25%: p=0.12; 100%: p=0.98; Wilcoxon signed-rank).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Iso-orientation adaptation differs significantly from cross-orientation adaptation at 25% contrast in putative excitatory cells in awake mice.

claim: There is no significant difference between iso- and cross-orientation adaptation at 100% contrast in putative excitatory cells in awake mice.
source: Same as f but in awake mice (239 cells; 25%: p=0.0082; 100%: p=0.14; Wilcoxon signed-rank).

claim: In the grating-relevant condition, the slope of adaptation does not significantly change from the first to the following sessions.

claim: In the grating-relevant condition, the mean response does not significantly change from the first to the following sessions.
